newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten warns against tinkering with HK freedoms.
newsitem.headline: Patten warns against tinkering with HK freedoms.

text.p: Just 100 days before the British colony of Hong Kong reverts to China, Governor Chris Patten paid a glowing tribute to the territory, which he likened to a Rolls Royce but warned against tinkering with the engine.

Speaking on Sunday in Radio Hong Kong's weekly Letter to Hong Kong broadcast, Patten dismissed arguments advocated by China and certain pro-Beijing politicians that rolling back some freedoms would not damage the community of 6.4 million people.
Gloomy predictions of chaos as Hong Kong entered the home straight to the handover had not materialised, he said.
"This is a sophisticated, moderate, responsible place. It wouldn't make much sense to damage the system that's helped create this mature stability," he said.
Patten said Hong Kong had prospered and grown used to its freedoms, of its independent civil service, of running its own financial affairs independently of Britain.
Views that Hong Kong would quickly adjust to a Singapore-style "smack of firm government, or whatever you care to call it", were dubious, he said.
"I happen to think myself that Hong Kong needs governing with a light touch. That you can't turn the clock back on what Hong Kong has become, any more than you can reverse the countdown."
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at the stroke of midnight on June 30, 1997.

China has promised the wealthy territory considerable autonomy in running its affairs, but plans to dilute key civil liberties laws and dissolve Hong Kong's elected legislature in favour of an appointed interim body, undoing democratic reforms introduced in the final years of British rule to Beijing's fury.
Hong Kong's democracy camp, the British and its allies in Europe and North America have urged China to reconsider.
Pro-Beijing officials argue the changes are mainly technical and will not materially damage Hong Kong freedoms.
"Hong Kong is, as I said recently, a smoothly functioning community. It's like a Rolls Royce," Patten said.
"All you need to do if you're in charge is to slip into the driving seat, switch on the ignition and away you go.

"I don't quite see the point of lifting the bonnet to tinker with the engine. That only raises worries about whether it will work so well, and whether you may be persuaded by some people to start stripping it down for spare parts."
